findings.title: Unpinned package executed on every start: crawlora-mcp
findings.detail: 'crawlora-mcp' launches crawlora-mcp through npx without a version. The client resolves the version at start time, so any future publish to that package name runs with your credentials. This is how postmark-mcp (Sept 2025) reached roughly 300 organisations.
findings.remediation: Pin an exact version and an integrity hash: "args": ["crawlora-mcp@<version>"] and drop the -y flag. Re-pin deliberately, after reviewing the diff.

findings.title: Description reads as instructions to the model (p=1.00): datasets_llms_item
findings.detail: The description of 'crawlora-mcp.datasets_llms_item' scores 1.00 on the instruction-detection model, and carries intent signals: hardcoded_recipient. Descriptions are documentation for a human, but they are delivered to the model as trusted context, so text that tells the model what to do is an attack surface rather than a description. The score is driven mainly by: hardcoded_recipient, entropy, log_len, imperative_density.

findings.title: Toxic flow within 'crawlora-mcp': executes commands + sends data outbound
findings.detail: 588 combination(s) exist where one tool executes commands and another sends data outbound. Neither tool is malicious on its own; together they executes commands and can reach the network, which is remote code execution with a delivery channel rather than a hint of one. Both sides live in the same server, which may well be by design; confirm it.
findings.remediation: Break the path, not the tools: scope the credential so the source tool cannot reach anything valuable, or require explicit user confirmation on the sink tool (destructiveHint / human-in-the-loop), or split the two capabilities across trust boundaries that cannot share a context window.

findings.title: Toxic flow within 'crawlora-mcp': reads credentials or secrets + sends data outbound
findings.detail: 1238 combination(s) exist where one tool reads credentials or secrets and another sends data outbound. Neither tool is malicious on its own; together they reads credentials and can send data to an address it controls. A single prompt is enough to turn 'summarise this config' into a credential leak. Both sides live in the same server, which may well be by design; confirm it.

findings.title: Mixed-script text in tool description: datasets_creators_search
findings.detail: 'crawlora-mcp.datasets_creators_search' contains Characters from the Cyrillic/Greek confusable set: ['а', 'в', 'о', 'р', 'у']. Homoglyphs let a description read correctly to a reviewer while presenting different codepoints to any matcher that looks for specific words.
findings.remediation: Normalise the text to ASCII; confirm the package source is what you think it is.

findings.title: No baseline supplied - drift detection is disabled
findings.detail: Without an approved snapshot the scanner cannot tell a tool that has always been there from one that appeared yesterday. The single most effective MCP control is the diff, and it needs a baseline to diff against.
findings.remediation: Run 'mcp-scrutiny baseline --config <file> --out mcp-baseline.json', commit the file, and pass it back with --baseline on every later scan.
